name: Computer Networks
blurb: One best video per subtopic, mostly from Jim Kurose, co-author of the standard networking textbook. Each comes with a deeper or hands-on alternative and a quick refresher. Watch the best pick, then do that subtopic's MCQs.
method:
• Best pick: the clearest correct explanation at interview depth. Most are Jim Kurose's own short lectures for Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, so they match the textbook your syllabus is built on.
  • Go deeper: hands-on or production-level detail, from Ben Eater (real packets on real wires), Hussein Nasser (how backends use TCP, HTTP and TLS) and others.
  • Quick / visual: short explanations for revision, such as Practical Networking's subnetting and packet-walk videos and 3Blue1Brown on Hamming codes.
  • Candidates came from about 5,000 YouTube links in Hacker News comments plus YouTube search for every subtopic. High-view exam channels lost when an English lecture explained the same idea more precisely; numericals are covered by the linked MCQs.

subtopics.name: Full courses
subtopics.note: Kurose's lectures follow his textbook chapter by chapter; work through them in order on his channel. Ben Eater's series shows the same layers with real hardware.

picks.title: 1.1 Introduction (reposted) - What is the Internet
picks.why: Start of the textbook author's own lecture series: about 50 videos of 10–30 minutes covering every chapter. Every best pick below except subnetting, TLS and proxies comes from it.

picks.title: Networking tutorial
picks.why: From voltages on a wire through Ethernet, IP, ARP and a full TCP connection, reading the actual bits at every layer. Nothing else makes the stack this concrete.

subtopics.name: OSI & TCP/IP Models
subtopics.note: What each layer is responsible for, encapsulation (segment, datagram, frame), and which devices work at which layer.

picks.title: 1.5 Layering, encapsulation
picks.why: Why networks are layered, the five-layer Internet stack against the seven-layer OSI model, and how headers wrap each other.

picks.title: How Data moves through the Internet - Networking Fundamentals
picks.why: Follows one request from your laptop to a server and back, naming the layer and device responsible at each step. Ideal for "what happens when…" questions.

picks.title: Packet Traveling - How Packets Move Through a Network
picks.why: Hosts, switches and routers, and what each one rewrites in a packet as it passes.

subtopics.name: Physical & Data Link Layer
subtopics.note: MAC addresses and ARP, switches and their learning tables, multiple-access protocols (ALOHA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA) and Ethernet framing.

picks.title: 6.3 Multiple Access links  and protocols
picks.why: Channel partitioning, random access (ALOHA, CSMA/CD) and taking-turns protocols, with the efficiency reasoning behind each.

picks.title: ARP: Mapping between IP and Ethernet | Networking tutorial (9 of 13)
picks.why: ARP requests and replies captured off a real network, so you see exactly how an IP address becomes a MAC address.

picks.title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) in less than 5 minutes
picks.why: ARP in four minutes for revision.

subtopics.name: Error Detection & Correction
subtopics.note: Parity, Internet checksum, CRC (and how to compute the remainder), Hamming distance and Hamming codes.

picks.title: 6.2 Error detection and correction
picks.why: Parity, two-dimensional parity, checksums and CRC side by side, so the trade-offs are clear.

picks.title: How do CRCs work?
picks.why: Builds CRC from polynomial division and shows why it catches burst errors. After this, CRC numericals are mechanical.

picks.title: But what are Hamming codes? The origin of error correction
picks.why: The best intuition for how parity bits can locate an error, not just detect it.

subtopics.name: Flow Control & ARQ
subtopics.note: Stop-and-wait, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat: sequence-number space, window sizes, utilisation and what happens on loss. Practise the numericals in the MCQs.

picks.title: 3.4-1 Principles of Reliable Data Transfer  (Part 1)
picks.why: Builds a reliable protocol step by step (checksums, ACKs, sequence numbers, timers), so every ARQ rule has a reason.

picks.title: 3.4-2 Principles of Reliable Data Transfer  (Part 2)
picks.why: Pipelining: Go-Back-N against Selective Repeat, window-size limits and the utilisation formula.

subtopics.name: IP Addressing & Subnetting
subtopics.note: CIDR notation, network/broadcast addresses, host counts, and splitting a block into subnets quickly by hand.

picks.title: What is Subnetting? - Subnetting Mastery - Part 1 of 7
picks.why: The clearest start on subnetting, from a CCIE-level instructor. The rest of his seven-part series builds real speed.

picks.title: How to solve ANY Subnetting Problems in 60 seconds or less - Subnetting Mastery - Part 3 of 7
picks.why: A reliable method for working out network, broadcast and host range under time pressure in an aptitude round.

picks.title: 4.3 The Internet Protocol, part 1
picks.why: The IPv4 datagram, addressing, CIDR and how hierarchical addressing enables route aggregation.

subtopics.name: NAT, IPv6, ICMP & Fragmentation
subtopics.note: How NAT rewrites ports, why IPv6 exists and what it changed, ICMP (ping and traceroute) and fragmentation fields (ID, MF flag, offset).

picks.title: 4.3 The Internet Protocol, part 2
picks.why: The second half of Kurose's IP section: getting an address, NAT and the move to IPv6.

picks.title: The Internet Protocol | Networking tutorial (8 of 13)
picks.why: Reads every IPv4 header field off a real packet: TTL, protocol, checksum and the fragmentation fields.

picks.title: 4 5 Middleboxes, Internet architecture
picks.why: NAT, firewalls and load balancers as middleboxes, and how they bend the end-to-end principle.

subtopics.name: Routing Algorithms & Protocols
subtopics.note: Link-state (Dijkstra, OSPF) against distance-vector (Bellman-Ford, RIP, count-to-infinity), and why the Internet uses BGP between autonomous systems.

picks.title: 5.2 Routing algorithms: link state routing
picks.why: Dijkstra as routers actually run it, with the oscillation problem and complexity.

picks.title: 5.2-2 Bellman Ford Distance Vector Routing (updated)
picks.why: Distance vector worked through table by table, including count-to-infinity and poisoned reverse.

picks.title: 5.4 BGP: the Border Gateway Protocol
picks.why: eBGP and iBGP, path attributes and policy routing: how the Internet's networks actually connect.

picks.title: EGP / IGP :: Distance Vector / Link State :: Dynamic Routing Protocols :: OSPF EIGRP BGP RIP IS-IS
picks.why: Sorts every routing protocol name into the right category in twelve minutes.

subtopics.name: TCP & UDP
subtopics.note: Ports and multiplexing, the TCP header, the 3-way handshake and 4-way teardown (TIME_WAIT), and when UDP is the better choice.

picks.title: 3.5-1 TCP Reliability, Flow Control, and Connection Management
picks.why: Sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmission timers, the handshake and connection close, all in one lecture.

picks.title: 3.3 Connectionless Transport: UDP
picks.why: What UDP gives you, what it doesn't, and the Internet checksum.

picks.title: TCP vs UDP Crash Course
picks.why: A backend engineer on how the TCP/UDP choice plays out in real servers: connection cost, head-of-line blocking, statefulness.

picks.title: TCP connection walkthrough | Networking tutorial (13 of 13)
picks.why: A real TCP connection from SYN to FIN in Wireshark, with every flag and sequence number explained.

subtopics.name: TCP Flow & Congestion Control
subtopics.note: Receive window vs congestion window, slow start, AIMD, fast retransmit/recovery, Tahoe vs Reno, and what CUBIC and BBR change.

picks.title: 3 7 TCP Congestion Control
picks.why: Slow start, congestion avoidance, AIMD, Tahoe vs Reno, CUBIC, and delay-based control, with the cwnd graphs interviewers sketch.

picks.title: 3.6 Principles of Congestion Control
picks.why: Why congestion collapse happens at all. Watch it first if the cwnd rules feel arbitrary.

picks.title: 3.5-2 TCP Reliability, Flow Control, and Congestion Control (part 2/2)
picks.why: Flow control with rwnd and fast retransmit: the half of the topic that's about the receiver, not the network.

picks.title: Slow Start vs Congestion Avoidance in TCP
picks.why: The two phases and the threshold between them, in ten minutes.

subtopics.name: HTTP & Web Protocols
subtopics.note: Requests, methods, status codes, persistent connections, cookies, caching, and what HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) fix.

picks.title: 2.2 The Web and HTTP (part 1)
picks.why: Non-persistent vs persistent connections with RTT counting, message formats, cookies and web caches.

picks.title: Hyper Text Transfer Protocol Crash Course - HTTP 1.0, 1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3
picks.why: Every HTTP version and the exact problem each one solved: pipelining, multiplexing, head-of-line blocking, QUIC.

picks.title: HTTP 1 Vs HTTP 2 Vs HTTP 3!
picks.why: A clean diagram-driven comparison for revision.

subtopics.name: DNS, DHCP, Email & FTP
subtopics.note: DNS hierarchy, iterative vs recursive resolution, record types and caching; the DHCP DORA exchange; SMTP vs POP3/IMAP; FTP's separate control connection.

picks.title: 2.4 The Domain Name System (DNS)
picks.why: Root, TLD and authoritative servers, iterative vs recursive queries, records and caching.

picks.title: DHCP Explained - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
picks.why: The Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge exchange and leases, animated.

subtopics.name: Network Security
subtopics.note: Symmetric vs public-key crypto, certificates and the chain of trust, the TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes, and common attacks.

picks.title: Transport Layer Security, TLS 1.2 and 1.3 (Explained by Example)
picks.why: Key exchange, why TLS 1.3 needs one fewer round trip, and forward secrecy, all worked by example.

picks.title: What are SSL/TLS Certificates? Why do we Need them? and How do they Work?
picks.why: Certificates, CAs and how a browser verifies a site: the trust half of HTTPS.

picks.title: SSL, TLS, HTTPS Explained
picks.why: The whole HTTPS handshake in one diagram for revision.

subtopics.name: Delays & Performance
subtopics.note: Transmission vs propagation vs queuing delay, throughput and the bottleneck link, the bandwidth-delay product. Practise the numericals in the MCQs.

picks.title: 1.4 Performance
picks.why: The four delay components, packet loss, throughput and the bottleneck link, with the formulas numericals use.

picks.title: 1.3 The network core
picks.why: Store-and-forward and packet vs circuit switching: the model the delay formulas come from.

subtopics.name: Web Infrastructure & Scenarios
subtopics.note: Forward vs reverse proxies, L4 vs L7 load balancing, CDNs, and stitching DNS + TCP + TLS + HTTP together for "what happens when you type a URL".

picks.title: Proxy vs. Reverse Proxy (Explained by Example)
picks.why: What each proxy hides, from whom, and what it's used for: caching, TLS termination, load balancing.

picks.title: Load balancing in Layer 4 vs Layer 7 with HAPROXY Examples
picks.why: What a load balancer can see and do at layer 4 vs layer 7, demonstrated with HAProxy.

picks.title: 2.6 Video Streaming and Content Distribution Networks
picks.why: How CDNs choose a server for you (DNS redirection) and adaptive streaming with DASH.
